title: The Ingredients of Successful Helping
overview: Egan's opening chapter sets out what helping is for and what makes it work. It begins with who helps (formal, professional and informal helpers), then explains why clients come (problem situations and unused opportunities) and the three outcome-focused goals of helping: life-enhancing outcomes, learning to help oneself, and a prevention mentality. The core of the chapter lists the ingredients of successful helping: the client and context, the person of the therapist, the relationship, dialogue, two-way feedback, the treatment model, problem management and decision making as human universals, and beliefs, values and ethics, illustrated through the case of Karl, a veteran with PTSD, and his counsellor Laura. It closes by asking helpers to embrace the uncertainty that runs through every ingredient and to move from smart to wise by facing the shadow side of helping.
objectives: Distinguish formal helpers, other professionals who help, and informal helpers.
Explain problem situations and unused opportunities as starting points of helping, including positive psychology and its critics.
Describe Egan's three outcome-focused goals of helping with examples.
List and explain each ingredient of successful helping and the research behind it.
Outline the Standard Problem-Management Framework and why it is a human universal and common factor.
Describe the rational decision-making model and its limitations, including Kahneman's two systems.
Discuss the role of beliefs, values, norms, ethics and morality, including positive and aspirational ethics.
Explain why uncertainty pervades helping and what is meant by the shadow side of helping.

sections.heading: Formal and Informal Helpers: A Very Brief History
sections.detailed:
Egan opens by noting that across history and across cultures people have held a deep belief that, under the right conditions, some people can help others come to grips with problems in living. The way this belief is expressed differs from culture to culture, but the belief itself is cross-cultural. In modern societies it has been institutionalised in a number of helping professions.

First set: formal helpers. In Western cultures counsellors, psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers and ministers of religion are among those whose official role is to help people manage the distressing problems of life. The book is addressed directly to this group.

Second set: professionals who help as part of another job. Organisational consultants, dentists, doctors, lawyers, nurses, probation officers, teachers, managers, supervisors, police officers and other service workers are specialists in their own fields, yet there is an expectation that they will also help the people they serve to handle problem situations. Egan's examples: teachers teach subjects to students who are growing physically, intellectually, socially and emotionally and facing developmental tasks and crises, so teachers are well placed to help students explore and deal with the problems of growing up, directly or indirectly. Managers and supervisors help workers cope with job performance, career development, workplace relationships and personal problems that affect their work. The book is addressed indirectly to this group.

Informal helpers. Beyond professionals, relatives, friends, acquaintances and even strangers on buses and planes help others with problems in living. Bartenders and hairdressers are often cited as examples. Friends help one another through hard times, and parents must manage their own marital problems while helping their children develop. Egan stresses that only a small fraction of the help given on any day comes from professionals; most people who seek help at all seek it from informal sources (Swindle, Heller, Pescosolido and Kikuzawa, 2000).

Self-help. Ultimately everyone must learn to help themselves cope with life's problems and crises, sometimes alone and sometimes with mostly informal help. Egan therefore presents the book as being about the basic ingredients of successful helping, meant to make the reader a better helper whichever category they belong to.
sections.simple: People everywhere believe some people can help others with life's problems. There are formal helpers (counsellors, psychologists, social workers), professionals who help as part of another job (teachers, doctors, managers), and informal helpers (friends, family, even strangers). Most help actually comes from informal sources, and in the end we all have to learn to help ourselves.
keyPoints: The belief that some people can help others with problems in living is cross-cultural and historical.
Formal helpers (counsellors, psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, ministers) are the book's direct audience.
Teachers, doctors, managers, police and similar professionals help as part of their jobs and are the indirect audience.
Most people who seek help turn to informal helpers such as friends, family, bartenders and hairdressers (Swindle et al., 2000).
Ultimately everyone must learn to help themselves.

sections.heading: What Helping Is About: Clients with Problem Situations and Unused Opportunities
sections.detailed:
Egan says helping is first about the person seeking help. He uses the word client rather than patient, to sidestep for now the debate about applying the medical model to helping (Wampold). To understand what helping is about, he asks two questions: why do people seek (or get sent for) help, and what are the main goals of helping? This section answers the first.

Problem situations. Clients come with crises, troubles, doubts, frustrations and concerns. These are not problems in the mathematical sense, because they stir emotional turmoil and rarely have clear-cut solutions. Egan prefers the term problem situations: complex, messy problems in living that the client is not handling well. They may be poorly defined; or well defined but the client does not know how to handle them; or the client feels short of resources; or attempted solutions have failed. Problem situations arise in our dealings with ourselves, with others, and with organisations and institutions. His list ranges from self-doubt, irrational fears, illness, addiction and failing marriages to job loss, acculturation stress, war trauma, catastrophic loss, midlife crisis, loneliness, domestic violence and racism. Sometimes others (teachers, supervisors, courts) refer or even mandate people into help.

The case of Martha. After losing a son, her job and her husband within six months, Martha became agitated, depressed and guilty and initially refused help. Her minister's gentle persistence led her to a church support group guided by a psychologist; through it she accepted help from her sons, saw herself as part of a grieving family, made friends and found a new job. Help came from many sources, and it let her tap her own unused strengths. Egan's point: nothing solved her losses. The goal of helping is not to solve problems but to help people manage them better or even transcend them by seizing new possibilities. Problems have an upside: they are opportunities for learning.

Missed opportunities and unused potential. A second starting point is clients who are not troubled so much as not as effective as they would like to be: people in dead-end jobs or bland marriages, without challenging goals, failing to live up to their values, or with dull interpersonal lives. The question is not what is going wrong but what could be better, since most of us use only a fraction of our potential. In the case of Carol, a burnt-out mental health worker, the counsellor noticed she felt best when consulting to other centres, helped her explore that opportunity, and she retrained in organisation development. Managing burnout and guilt was achieved by developing an opportunity; the helper was a catalyst and Carol took the lead.

Positive psychology. Developing unused potential can be called a positive psychology goal. Seligman and Csikszentmihalyi (2000) argued that the field focused too much on pathology and too little on strength and virtue, on nurturing what is best rather than only fixing what is broken. Topics include well-being, happiness, hope, optimism, love, forgiveness, courage, creativity, wisdom and spirituality. Ince (2009) called positive psychology the science of satisfaction. For Egan, helping is not just fixing but enabling clients to design and redesign their lives using overlooked inner resources (strengths, values, beliefs, resilience); fixing and redesigning often blend, and sometimes transcending problems is better than working through them.

Cautions. Positive psychology is not an "everything will be fine" approach. Richard Lazarus (2000) warned it could sink to a Pollyanna level of simplistic, quasi-religious thinking and become a passing fad. Research by McNulty and Fincham (2012) challenges inflated claims. Still, helping at its best engenders hope, and hopeful clients are more likely to reach life-enhancing goals.
sections.simple: People come for help for two reasons: problem situations they are not handling well, or opportunities and potential they are not using. Helping does not "solve" problems; it helps people manage or rise above them. Positive psychology (Seligman and Csikszentmihalyi) reminds helpers to build strengths, not just fix weaknesses, though Lazarus warned against making it a shallow fad.
keyPoints: Egan uses 'client' rather than 'patient' to avoid the medical-model dispute.
Problem situations are messy, emotionally charged problems in living with no clear-cut solutions.
Missed opportunities and unused potential are a second starting point: not what is wrong, but what could be better.
The goal is to help clients manage or transcend problems, not to 'solve' them; problems are learning opportunities.
Positive psychology (Seligman and Csikszentmihalyi, 2000) balances pathology with strengths; Lazarus (2000) warned against a Pollyanna fad.
Helping at its best builds hope, which predicts reaching goals.

sections.heading: The Three Principal Outcome-Focused Goals of Helping: Goal One, Life-Enhancing Outcomes
sections.detailed:
Egan complains that much of the helping literature is about models, methods and skills and much less about outcomes, even though helping should mainly be about life-enhancing outcomes for clients. Duncan, Miller and colleagues (2010) promote "client-directed and outcome-informed" (CDOI) helping to restore this balance. Because helpers do not solve or manage clients' problems for them, clients must become agents of change in their own lives, and change means outcomes: problems managed and opportunities identified and developed.

Tim's case. Tim, a decent ordinary teenager, was cyberbullied by classmates, became anxious and withdrew socially. His parents supported him, arranged a school counsellor and met the principal, who announced the bullying was being investigated; it stopped. The Parents Association issued a zero-tolerance statement. Research by Faris and Ennett (2011) and Faris and Felmlee (2011) showed adolescent psychological and social aggression was far more widespread than realised, with over half of students involved as aggressors, victims or both. Outcomes: Tim's anxiety eased, friends confided in him, his relationship with his parents became more mutual, and the school took aggression seriously. He got his life back. Egan invites readers to find all three goals in this case.

Goal One: help clients manage their problems in living more effectively and develop unused or underused resources and opportunities more fully, at the service of life-enhancing outcomes. Helpers succeed to the extent that clients, through client-helper interaction, see the need to manage problems and develop opportunities more effectively. Egan deliberately stops short of saying clients will actually do so: helpers influence but do not control outcomes, and clients can choose whether to live more effectively.

Corollary: helping is about constructive change. Outcomes studied in therapy research include satisfaction, symptom reduction, constructive change as seen by self or others, and improved end-point functioning (Lunnen, Ogles and Pappas, 2008). Helping is an "-ing" word, a set of activities, but those activities matter only if they lead to valued outcomes. "We had a good session" must translate into more effective living: fears reduced, confidence replacing self-doubt, addictions conquered, a better job, a renewed marriage, a battered wife finding courage to leave. Gladding (2005), a past president of the American Counseling Association, describes constructive counselling as clients growing, making purposeful decisions, dropping destructive behaviour, taking charge of themselves, using strengths and practising new behaviours.

Palpable impact. Kazdin (2006) urges moving beyond statistically and even clinically significant change to change with visible impact on daily life; for a child with conduct disorder this means no longer hitting family members, doing homework, not stealing, and playing gently with an infant sibling. Driscoll (1984) showed the same with Andrea, a battered woman: helping produced a chain of outcomes, first self-worth and confidence, then assertiveness replacing passivity, then established rights and better relationships, and finally seeing herself as an agent rather than a patient. Andrea needed outcomes, not merely good sessions.
sections.simple: Helping should be judged by real results in the client's life, not by "good sessions". Goal One is to help clients manage problems and develop unused opportunities so their lives improve. Helpers influence but cannot control these outcomes; the change has to be palpable in daily life, as Kazdin and Driscoll's examples show.
keyPoints: The literature over-emphasises methods; Duncan, Miller et al. (2010) promote client-directed, outcome-informed (CDOI) helping.
Goal One: manage problems and develop unused resources and opportunities for life-enhancing outcomes.
Helpers do not control outcomes; clients choose whether to live more effectively.
Helping is an '-ing' word whose activities are valuable only if they lead to outcomes (Lunnen, Ogles and Pappas, 2008; Gladding, 2005).
Kazdin (2006) wants palpable everyday impact beyond statistical or clinical significance; Driscoll's Andrea shows a chain of outcomes.

sections.heading: The Three Principal Outcome-Focused Goals of Helping: Goals Two and Three
sections.detailed:
Goal Two: Learning how to help oneself. Help clients become better at helping themselves in everyday life. Clients are often poor problem solvers, and whatever skill they have tends to vanish in a crisis. Egan quotes G. A. Miller, Galanter and Pribram (1960): in ordinary life we muddle along doing what is habitual, and an ordinary person almost never tackles a problem systematically unless specifically educated to do so. Many people are still not so educated, and they are equally poor at spotting and developing opportunities. Society has not ensured that children learn core life skills such as problem management, opportunity development, sensible decision making and interpersonal relating. So if clients are to leave better able to manage on their own, helpers must pass on working knowledge and skills. Nelson-Jones (2005) puts it that the purpose of counselling skills is to make clients more skilled in their own right; counsellors are skilled only to the extent they succeed in "skilling" clients. Hence Egan describes his book as fundamentally about a problem-management and opportunity-development process that clients themselves can use, making them better problem managers, opportunity developers, decision makers and responsible agents of change.

Goal Three: Developing a prevention mentality. Help clients develop an action-oriented prevention mentality. Just as doctors and dentists want patients to prevent illness, skilled helpers want clients to anticipate problem situations rather than only manage them once they occur. The economics of prevention are extraordinary in marriage and relationships; in health care, by some estimates, each dollar on prevention saves ten on cure. Good nutrition and exercise prevent complaints and free energy for other pursuits. But prevention is inherently problematic: when it works, nothing bad happens, so its benefits are invisible, whereas cure is tangible and therefore more attractive. Helpers must help clients make prevention attractive to themselves.

Ingrid and Carlos. Four years into marriage they arrived blaming each other over money, sex and child rearing. The counsellor used the pinch-crunch model (Sherwood and Glidewell, 1973): small unspoken annoyances ("pinches") are saved up until they explode into major blowups ("crunches"). Ingrid resented Carlos's spending on himself while he resented hers; Carlos felt Ingrid was less spontaneous sexually yet she was jealous of his glances; neither spoke up. The counsellor did three things: (1) helped them defuse their most acute problem, child care; (2) taught them the problem-management approach and walked them through it on their financial problems so they had skills for the future (Goal Two); (3) from a prevention angle, showed them that saving up pinches leads to crunches and that they should use the decent communication skills they already had, but did not use with each other, to defuse pinches early. He also taught that fair-minded negotiation is part of everyday life, not just diplomacy, and pointed them to resources. The case thus shows all three goals working together.
sections.simple: Goal Two is to make clients better at helping themselves by teaching them problem-management skills, since most people never learn to solve problems systematically. Goal Three is to build a prevention mindset so clients head off problems before they blow up. Prevention is hard to sell because its benefits are invisible, as the pinch-crunch case of Ingrid and Carlos shows.
keyPoints: Goal Two: help clients become better at helping themselves in everyday life.
Most people never approach problems systematically unless taught (Miller, Galanter and Pribram, 1960).
Nelson-Jones (2005): counsellors are skilled only to the extent that they skill their clients.
Goal Three: develop an action-oriented prevention mentality; prevention is invaluable but its benefits are invisible.
Pinch-crunch model (Sherwood and Glidewell, 1973): saved-up small annoyances explode into major crises.
The Ingrid and Carlos case illustrates all three goals.

sections.heading: The Ingredients of Successful Helping
sections.detailed:
Egan now asks what basic elements are found in successful helping, defining success as life-enhancing outcomes for clients. Each ingredient can be named and described separately, but in real helping they are interactive, dynamic and overlapping.

Common factors versus ingredients. Many writers use "common factors" for the essential elements of successful therapy, and much research over the past decade has tried to identify them (Duncan; Duncan, Miller, Wampold and Hubble, 2010; Norcross, 2011; Wampold, 2010). Egan's elements are mostly research-based but go beyond the usual lists, which is why he prefers the word "ingredient" to "factor". He admits not everyone will accept his list, order or evidence. He borrows Miller, Hubble, Duncan and Wampold's (2010) description of common factors: not fixed or neatly additive, but interdependent, fluid and dynamic. He lays out his reasoning and lets the reader and profession judge, noting that the social sciences study messy, hard-to-predict behaviour, so debate and uncertainty are part of the field.

The list. The first ingredient has already been discussed: the life-enhancing outcomes clients seek. The remaining ingredients are:
1. The client and the contextual factors of the client's life.
2. The person of the therapist.
3. The helping relationship.
4. The therapeutic dialogue between client and helper.
5. Two-way feedback between client and helper.
6. The model or method of treatment and the assumptions behind it.
7. The standard problem-management process as a human universal.
8. Decision making as a human universal.
9. The beliefs, values, norms, ethics and morality that drive human behaviour.

All are useful only to the extent that, alone or together, they contribute to life-enhancing outcomes.

Karl's case. To illustrate, Egan introduces Karl, a veteran of Iraq and Afghanistan whose squad was ambushed and two best friends killed. About a month after returning to base he developed the full range of PTSD symptoms (nightmares, flashbacks, anxiety, depression, irritability, insomnia, social avoidance, poor concentration, emotional numbness) and began ruminating over poor pre-military decisions: skipping college, ending a relationship, drifting from God. He felt guilty, including about his friends' deaths, and saw a life of misery ahead, though he was not suicidal. Discharged honourably, he resisted help ("I'm no psycho"), took medication only intermittently, and refused a VA therapist because he wanted distance from the military. He finally agreed to see Laura, a counsellor at a clinic attached to a Christian hospital near an army camp. The case runs through the rest of the chapter.
sections.simple: Success in helping means real, life-enhancing outcomes. Egan lists the ingredients that produce them: the client, the therapist, the relationship, dialogue, two-way feedback, the treatment model, problem management, decision making, and beliefs-values-ethics. He calls them ingredients rather than common factors because his list goes beyond the usual research lists, and they all interact.
keyPoints: Success = life-enhancing outcomes; outcomes are the first ingredient.
Egan prefers 'ingredient' to 'common factor' because his list goes beyond standard research lists.
Ingredients are interdependent, fluid and dynamic, not neatly additive (Miller, Hubble, Duncan and Wampold, 2010).
Nine further ingredients: client and context, therapist, relationship, dialogue, two-way feedback, treatment model, problem management, decision making, beliefs-values-norms-ethics-morality.
Karl, a veteran with PTSD, and his counsellor Laura illustrate the ingredients.

sections.heading: The Client and the Contextual Factors of the Client's Life
sections.detailed:
The client, searching for life-enhancing outcomes, is the first and most important ingredient (Bohart and Tallman, 2010). Yet therapy research has concentrated on treatment models and shortchanged what clients bring, which is odd because research shows that clients and what they bring account for most of the success or failure of helping (Duncan, 2010; Orlinsky, Rønnestad and Willutzki, 2004).

What clients bring. Clients arrive with their own version of humanity in all its simplicity and complexity. Egan's partial list includes: the problem situations and concerns, of varying severity, for which they want help; successful or failed attempts to deal with problems or opportunities; the past, insofar as it affects them now; life expectations and aspirations, realistic or distorted, and related disappointments; skills, strengths and resources; general emotional state; hopes, fears and expectations about therapy; openness and readiness for change; willingness to work at change; reluctance or resistance; ability to collaborate; sense of right and wrong and personal ethics; cultural beliefs, values and norms, especially their own version of the dominant culture; their whole web of relationships, especially those tied to the problem; interpersonal communication skills; blind spots; and external factors that both block and support change.

Implications. All of these are relevant to Karl. Because people are complex, helpers need to identify the key factors for each client, or better still, help clients discover them. In the end the quality of the client's participation is the major determinant of outcome, so Karl needs a therapist who helps him give his best. Clients are, or should be, in the driver's seat for managing their lives, and therapists must help them get there and stay there. Following Duncan and Sparks (2010), Egan says that if there are heroes in therapy they are clients, not therapists. Karl is responsible for change; his helper is a catalyst.
sections.simple: The client is the most important ingredient: research shows clients and what they bring account for most of therapy's success. Clients bring problems, history, strengths, emotions, culture, relationships, readiness for change and blind spots. The client should be in the driver's seat, with the helper as catalyst.
keyPoints: The client is the first and most important ingredient (Bohart and Tallman, 2010).
Clients and what they bring account for most of the success or failure of helping (Duncan, 2010; Orlinsky et al., 2004).
Clients bring problems, past attempts, history, expectations, strengths, emotions, readiness, resistance, ethics, culture, relationships, skills, blind spots and external factors.
Quality of client participation is the major determinant of outcome.
Clients belong in the driver's seat; they are the heroes, the helper a catalyst (Duncan and Sparks, 2010).

sections.heading: The Person of the Therapist
sections.detailed:
Research has focused heavily on client problems and treatments, the stuff of abnormal psychology, while relatively little has examined the capabilities and characteristics of therapists (Beutler et al., 2004). Still, some things are known: the person of the therapist matters more than the treatment method (Crits-Christoph et al., 1991, 2006; Miller, Hubble, Duncan and Wampold, 2010; Wampold and Brown, 2005), and some therapists are better than others (Okiishi, Lambert, Nielsen and Ogles, 2003). The real question is what makes them better.

Wampold's list (2011), adapted by Egan. An effective therapist: has strong interpersonal skills expressing acceptance, warmth and empathy; builds trust so the client feels understood and hopeful; does their part to form a collaborative working alliance and agree on goals; understands the client's condition and offers a plausible explanation of the distress; understands the client in every relevant context (cultural, social, economic, political); has a flexible approach or treatment plan and explains it clearly; is believable and persuasive without robbing the client of autonomy or dignity; collaborates in monitoring progress and the client's view of helping; sets up a formal or informal feedback system; adjusts the process based on evolving understanding, feedback and signs of reluctance; fosters a realistic sense of possibility, hope and optimism; does not avoid difficult issues but handles them tactfully; understands self and self-discloses only when it helps; knows the best research on the client's personality, problems, context and treatments; is committed to professional self-improvement; and grasps the key ingredients of therapy and can tailor them collaboratively to client outcomes.

Why Laura? There is no single right mix, so Egan personalises the list by describing why, as a client, he would choose Laura: she adapts the ingredients to his needs rather than her theories, has no preset formula, is smart and competent without flaunting it, wears professionalism lightly, is fully present, respectful and street smart, communicates well and helps him communicate when he cannot, understands his values, neither cudgels nor coddles, invites him to explore the consequences of decisions, acts as a catalyst rather than an advice-giver, keeps the problem-management framework in the background as the "geography" of helping, collaborates as a team, admits mistakes, values feedback as a two-way street (reviewing progress at the start and evaluating each session at the end), invites him to review his commitment, and explores incentives and obstacles honestly.

Different clients, different preferences. In one study (Murphy, Cramer and Lillie, 1984) clients mainly from the lower socioeconomic class wanted advice, real interest, encouragement and reassurance, understanding and the instilling of hope. The principle remains: within reason, tailor the ingredients to the client's needs and preferences, without indulging the client.

What therapists want. Barry Duncan (2011) asks this and answers that it is not money or fame. Citing Orlinsky and Rønnestad (2005), therapists stay in the profession mainly because they value connecting deeply with clients and helping them improve, and they want to keep learning; they find satisfaction in deepening their understanding of themselves, clients, the profession and the world.
sections.simple: The therapist as a person matters more than the treatment method, and some therapists are clearly better than others. Wampold's list says effective therapists are warm, empathic, trustworthy, collaborative, flexible, feedback-oriented, hopeful, self-aware, research-informed and always improving. Egan's ideal, Laura, tailors everything to the client and treats helping as teamwork.
keyPoints: Little research has studied therapist characteristics (Beutler et al., 2004).
The person of the therapist matters more than the method (Crits-Christoph et al.; Wampold and Brown, 2005); some therapists are better (Okiishi et al., 2003).

Wampold's (2011) list: interpersonal skill, trust, alliance, plausible explanation, contextual understanding, flexible plan, feedback, hope, tact, self-understanding, research knowledge, self-improvement.
Laura illustrates a tailored, collaborative, catalytic, feedback-driven helper.
Lower-SES clients wanted advice, interest, reassurance, understanding and hope (Murphy, Cramer and Lillie, 1984).
Therapists stay for deep connection and continued learning, not money (Orlinsky and Rønnestad, 2005).

sections.heading: The Helping Relationship
sections.detailed:
Research identifies the quality of the client-helper relationship as the second most important ingredient after client factors (Muran and Barber, 2010; Norcross, 2011). When client and helper are a collaborative team the three goals are more likely to be achieved. The therapist's intelligence and competence produce results only when channelled into a collaborative relationship, and that will not happen unless clients also do their part. Client and therapist together, through dialogue, orchestrate the mix of ingredients that leads to targeted outcomes.

The APA Task Force. The American Psychological Association Interdivisional Task Force on Evidence-Based Therapy Relationships, chaired by John C. Norcross (Norcross, 2010, 2011; Norcross and Wampold, 2011), reached a range of conclusions about the relationship. Instead of listing them, Egan shows how they might shape Laura's thinking about Karl:
- Make building and focusing the relationship a top priority, keeping it tied to the main work of managing Karl's problems.
- The relationship will contribute more to outcomes than any particular approach.
- Ensure Karl understands and buys into the problem-management approach, and adapt it to him without compromising professional standards; they co-own the approach and Karl has a say in everything.
- Any programme loses power if the relationship is poor; even proven programmes for anxiety, depression or PTSD must be co-owned and collaboratively implemented, not applied like a technician.
- The relationship pervades every aspect of treatment; skills come alive only through it. Karl is not an anaesthetised patient having an appendectomy.
- Understand Karl from his point of view even when he might benefit from challenge; avoid hostility, criticism, rejection and blame.
- No formula fits everyone: some clients feel shortchanged without challenge while others resent even tactful invitations to self-challenge. Everything must help Karl become a partner.

Caution. The Task Force itself warned that its findings should be read in light of its acknowledged limitations; similar caution applies to all social-science findings. So Laura must stay flexible and take cues from Karl. The relationship is discussed further in Chapter 2.
sections.simple: After the client, the relationship is the most important ingredient. Skills and methods only work when delivered through a collaborative partnership. The APA Task Force led by Norcross supports this, but cautioned that its findings have limits, so helpers must stay flexible.
keyPoints: The relationship is the second most important ingredient after client factors (Muran and Barber, 2010; Norcross, 2011).
Therapist competence produces results only through a collaborative relationship.
APA Interdivisional Task Force on Evidence-Based Therapy Relationships, chaired by Norcross.
Skills and techniques are delivered through the relationship; programmes should be co-owned, not applied like a technician.
Avoid hostility, criticism, rejection and blame; no single formula fits every client.
The Task Force cautioned that its findings have limitations.

sections.heading: Communication Skills at the Service of Dialogue
sections.detailed:
Communication is at the heart of any relationship, and helpers need a range of communication skills to collaborate with clients. Part II of the book covers attending, listening, understanding what clients say about themselves, responding with understanding, helping clients explore concerns more fully, helping them stay focused, and helping them develop new perspectives on problem situations and unused opportunities.

Therapeutic dialogue. Helper-client conversations should be a therapeutic or helping dialogue (Knapp, 2007; Paré and Lysack, 2004; Seikkula and Trimble, 2005). Interpersonal communication competence means not only being good at individual skills but marshalling them in the service of dialogue.

When clients are poor communicators. Ideally clients would also have these skills and be able to weave them into dialogue, but often they do not; many are in trouble precisely because they cannot build and maintain healthy relationships nourished by good communication. Helpers then use their own skills to help clients engage in dialogue, without ever being condescending. How to do this is the subject of Part II.
sections.simple: Good communication is the core of the helping relationship. Helpers need skills like attending, listening, responding with understanding and probing, and must use them to build a real two-way dialogue. When clients communicate poorly, helpers use their own skills to draw them into dialogue without talking down to them.
keyPoints: Communication is at the heart of every relationship.
Skills: attending, listening, understanding, empathic responding, helping exploration, focusing, new perspectives.
Conversations should be a therapeutic dialogue (Knapp, 2007; Paré and Lysack, 2004; Seikkula and Trimble, 2005).
Competence means marshalling individual skills in the service of dialogue.
Many clients are poor communicators; helpers help them engage without condescension.

sections.heading: Two-Way Feedback Between Client and Helper
sections.detailed:
Feedback is a critical factor in the helping dialogue (Miller, Duncan et al., 2006). Two things must be monitored continually: progress toward life-enhancing outcomes, and how far sessions are contributing to them.

Questions about sessions: How are we doing? What is going right? What mistakes are we making? How can sessions be more productive? How can we collaborate better?
Questions about client progress: What does progress look like? Am I getting to the heart of the problem? Do I know what a resolution would look like? What are my goals and how can I clarify them? What actions must I take and how do I start? What obstacles am I meeting? What do I need to persist?

Duncan's feedback system. Both kinds of feedback have been studied (Duncan, 2010; Lambert, 2010). Duncan and colleagues developed a simple system of two brief surveys. The first, at the start of each session, has clients rate four areas: personal well-being; family and close relationships; work, school and friendships; and general sense of well-being. Given in the first session it jump-starts the process and provides a baseline for measuring between-session progress. The second, near the end of each session, measures within-session satisfaction by rating the relationship, whether the session addressed the right topics and goals, how well the approach fits the client, and overall satisfaction. Ideally the surveys stimulate dialogue, keep the client in the driver's seat and make sessions and between-session behaviour more productive.

Karl and Laura. Karl dismissed the forms as "playing games". Laura did not push; she made feedback a seamless part of dialogue, asking near the end "How do you think we're doing?" and tentatively sharing highlights until both agreed they were "feeling our way". She also suggested a "buddy" arrangement like Twelve-Step programmes, pairing Karl with a veteran who had come out the other side, something therapeutic rather than therapy. At the start of sessions she explores his progress, and at the end reviews what he learned and must do "out there". Miller et al. (2010) see such feedback as telling clients that their input matters and treatment will be modified for them. By the fourth session Karl said the informal feedback was working for him.

Feedback from helper to client. Most research concerns client feedback. Should helpers give feedback on clients' collaboration or between-session behaviour? This is a form of challenge, raising questions about whether it removes clients from the driver's seat or is criticism. Egan's view (developed in Part II): helping is inescapably a two-way social-influence process that neither removes the client from the driver's seat nor makes the helper a victim of client whims, and clients never invited to challenge themselves are shortchanged.
sections.simple: Helpers and clients should keep checking two things: whether the client is making progress and whether sessions are helping. Duncan's system uses two short surveys, one at the start and one at the end of each session. Laura adapted by building feedback into conversation when Karl rejected the forms. Feedback also flows from helper to client as a form of challenge.
keyPoints: Monitor progress toward outcomes and the usefulness of sessions (Miller, Duncan et al., 2006).
Duncan's system: an opening survey of four life areas (baseline, between-session progress) and a closing survey of session satisfaction.
Surveys aim to spark dialogue and keep the client in the driver's seat.
Laura made feedback informal when Karl rejected forms, and suggested a Twelve-Step style buddy.
Helper-to-client feedback is a form of challenge; helping is a two-way social-influence process.

sections.heading: The Treatment Approach and Its Methods and Techniques
sections.detailed:
There are dozens, perhaps hundreds, of helping approaches. To ask which is right, Egan offers a thought experiment. Ten therapists each practise a different approach: behaviour therapy, rational-emotive-behaviour therapy, narrative, emotion-focused, reality, person-centred, brief dynamic, cognitive behavioural, existential-humanistic and relational-cultural therapy (each the subject of an APA Books introductory series volume). Each has ten comparable clients, and all hundred clients succeed in managing their problems. Since ten different approaches produced equal success, the approach cannot be the main vehicle of success.

Better question. Instead of "Which approach is most effective?" Egan asks "What do successful therapists have in common?" His answer: they can tailor the essential ingredients of successful therapy to their clients and work collaboratively with them.

The method still matters. Research shows the treatment method is not the main driver of success (Wampold, 2010), but it remains important. A model organises and focuses both client and helper resources. It must have substance and face validity (it must make sense and look likely to work). The therapist must believe in it and be skilled and comfortable with it; the client must see it as reasonable and collaborate in carrying it out. Execution draws on all the other ingredients.

Tailoring. Research on "bona fide" psychotherapies for PTSD (Benish, Imel and Wampold, 2007) shows each has merit but one may suit a given client better than others. PTSD clients are not homogeneous, so tailoring is essential for Karl.
sections.simple: Many different therapy approaches work about equally well, so the approach itself is not the main reason for success. What successful therapists share is the ability to tailor the ingredients of therapy to each client and collaborate. Still, a sensible model the therapist and client both believe in helps organise the work.
keyPoints: There are dozens or hundreds of approaches; Egan's ten-therapist thought experiment shows equal success across approaches.
Ask what successful therapists share: tailoring the ingredients to clients and collaborating.
Method is not the main driver of success (Wampold, 2010) but organises and focuses resources.
A model needs face validity, therapist belief and skill, and client acceptance.
Bona fide PTSD therapies all have merit, but tailoring is essential (Benish, Imel and Wampold, 2007).

sections.heading: Problem Management: A Human Universal and a Common Factor
sections.detailed:
The approach highlighted in the book is one embedded in every other approach, already familiar to clients, and usable as a tool to borrow treatments from other approaches: the Standard Problem-Management Framework. It poses four questions clients ask in seeking life-enhancing outcomes:
1. What's going on? What problems, concerns or undeveloped opportunities should I work on? This helps clients spell out their current picture (Stage I).
2. What does a better future look like? What do I want my life to look like, what changes and goals would manage my problems and develop opportunities? This helps clients paint their preferred picture (Stage II).
3. How do I get there? What plan and actions will turn the preferred picture into reality? This is the way forward (Stage III).
4. How do I make it all happen? How do I turn plans and goals into action that yields results with impact, and persevere? This is the Action Arrow, the ongoing challenge of implementation.

Figure 1.1 turns these questions into three "stages" and an implementation arrow. Egan puts "stage" in quotation marks because its sequential overtones mislead: in practice the stages overlap and interact, and helping, like life, is less logical than the models describing it.

Embedded in people. Everyone faces problems and has unused opportunities, so the approach is recognised worldwide. It appears to be what McCrae and Costa (1997) call a "human universal" or what Norenzayan and Heine (2005) call a "psychological universal". People do not so much learn it as recognise it; in Orlinsky and Howard's (1987) term it is a "generic" helping framework. People often say "I know that", but many never actually use it. Egan describes presenting an early version to about 300 students and faculty in Tanzania: after a three-day seminar they said the communication skills would need cultural modification but the problem-management process was very useful. This has been repeated on every continent. Norenzayan and Heine argue universality is compelling when a phenomenon is identifiable across many diverse cultures. Still, the model must be adapted to cultures and to individuals within them, requiring diversity sensitivity (Chapter 2).

Embedded in therapy. Few approaches explicitly talk about problem management and opportunity development, yet all use its concepts directly or indirectly: identifying and exploring problems, unused strengths, goals, action plans, and obstacles to carrying them out. So Egan considers it a common factor found in all successful helping. In Part III it is the primary treatment approach and organiser of the ingredients (Chapter 8 details it). Some versions omit the Stage II question about the desired future; the shortened "What is my problem and what can I do about it?" works for a broken refrigerator but not for human problems. A married couple must ask what kind of marriage they want before asking how to create it.
sections.simple: Egan's core approach is the Standard Problem-Management Framework: What's going on (current picture)? What do I want (preferred picture)? How do I get there (way forward)? And how do I make it happen (action arrow)? It is a human universal recognised across cultures and used, openly or not, by all therapies, which makes it a common factor.
keyPoints: Four questions: current picture, preferred picture, way forward, implementation (Action Arrow).
Shown in Figure 1.1 as three overlapping 'stages' plus an implementation arrow; stages are not strictly sequential.
A human universal (McCrae and Costa, 1997), psychological universal (Norenzayan and Heine, 2005) and generic model (Orlinsky and Howard, 1987).
Tanzania seminar: communication skills need cultural adaptation, but the process itself was useful.
All therapies use problem-management concepts, so it is a common factor.
Skipping Stage II (the preferred future) loses richness; human problems need an imagined better future.

sections.heading: Decision Making: A Psychological Universal and a Common Factor
sections.detailed:
Each day we make many small decisions and occasionally big ones (whether to pursue other relationships, which cancer treatment to choose at 80, whether to confront a belittling boss). Clients are decision makers too: they often must make hard decisions, deal with fallout from poor past ones, or are afraid to decide at all. Because problem management deals with options, and decision making means choosing among options, decision making lies at the heart of helping; the two are often written about together (Adair, 2010). Clients decide whether to come, what to talk about, which issues to work on, goals, plans, finding the courage to act, telling the helper what works, and persevering. They bring a decision-making style, and understanding it helps the helper be a catalyst.

Egan outlines the Newtonian or rational approach (Baron, 2001; Galotti, 2002; Hammond, Keeney and Raiffa, 1999; and others), warning that real decision making is closer to the messiness of relativity and quantum mechanics.

1. Problem identification and information gathering. Start with an issue and gather relevant information, framing it accurately. A prostate cancer patient must learn the type, aggressiveness, likely progression, treatments, side effects, consequences of no treatment and second opinions, via Internet, books, doctors and other patients; information does not provide ready-made answers. In therapy problems are murkier. Karl recognises that being a loner, out of community, is part of his problem; he recalls being fairly gregarious though somewhat introverted, passive in groups, and close to a few army friends, concluding that being out of community is not good for him.

2. Analysis. Process the information: analyse, discuss, reflect, immerse oneself. Good processing clarifies the range of choices, for instance by weighing advantages and disadvantages, which assumes criteria for comparing alternatives. Karl's upside-downside analysis showed that the "upside" of passivity was self-centred, making him more parasite than contributor, whereas being somewhat introverted had a real upside: listening well and contributing thoughtfully. He discusses this with Laura.

3. Making a choice. Commit to an internal or external action based on the analysis. Anita decides to sue for custody and has her lawyer file the papers. Rational rules help, such as asking whether a choice will get everything or only part of what one wants. Values also enter, since values are criteria for decisions; Anita values fairness and will make reasonable demands. Karl admits he has become comfortable but not happy as a loner, the beginning of a decision to get back into community.

4. Follow through. Real decision making ends in action; otherwise it is wishful thinking. Karl accepts Laura's earlier offer to talk with a veteran who came out the other side, a buddy with substance, a start on his own kind of normalisation.

The shadow of decision making. The rational process is not the stuff of everyday life; people often undermine themselves by how they decide, even on important matters (Kahneman, 2012; Lehrer, 2009). Helpers do not decide for clients but help them make life-enhancing rather than life-limiting decisions, face decisions they avoid, and explore consequences. Helpers also face many choices in how they interact with clients, and understanding what influences those choices is key self-knowledge.
sections.simple: Helping is full of decisions, so decision making is a core ingredient. The rational model has four steps: identify the problem and gather information, analyse options, make a choice, and follow through with action. Real-life decisions are messier, so helpers help clients make life-enhancing choices and face the ones they avoid.
keyPoints: Problem management is about options; decision making (choosing among options) is at the heart of helping (Adair, 2010).
Clients bring a decision-making style; understanding it makes the helper a better catalyst.
Rational (Newtonian) model: problem identification and information gathering, analysis, making a choice, follow through.
Values act as criteria for choosing; decisions without action are wishful thinking.
Everyday decision making is messier; people often undermine themselves (Kahneman, 2012; Lehrer, 2009).
Helpers help clients make life-enhancing decisions and must understand their own decision influences.

sections.heading: The Beliefs-Values-Norms-Ethics-Morality Factors That Drive Human Behavior
sections.detailed:
If helping is to be a social-civilising and not just an individual-enhancement process, it must be value-driven and ethical, so morality and ethics are key ingredients. Egan has been criticised for not including a longer ethics section; his reply is that ethics is so important that a brief overview would send the wrong message. Every training programme should include a full ethics course, and beyond the ACA and APA codes there are excellent texts (Knapp, 2012; Welfel, 2013).

An intellectual challenge. The beliefs-values-norms-ethics-morality package challenges the helping professions (Mikulincer and Shaver, 2012). The professions strive to be scientific, yet these concepts and the cultures they sit in are not scientific terms. Science can study them as behaviour and show the social usefulness of shared patterns, but cannot prove their validity, nor prove or disprove God and religious moral injunctions. Egan recalls a TV debate in which an atheist scientist conceded everyone needs a moral compass, at which point social pragmatism replaced science. The APA wants science-based treatments yet also enforces a strict ethical code.

Sources of morality. Many find ethics in religion: Judaism, Christianity and Islam all have extensive moral codes, similar but with differences (for example, variations on "Do not kill"). Others turn to culture, defined as the interactive shared beliefs, values and norms of a group; because cultures differ, their codes differ (one culture condemns revenge, another may see it as a duty in some circumstances). Others see morality as a bio-social-evolutionary phenomenon (Brooks, 2012; Churchland, 2011; Wilson, 1993). Still others take a pragmatic view: if 7 billion people are to live in harmony, commonsense rules are needed, backed by laws. In many ways beliefs, values, norms, ethics and moral principles are choices, not givens. The common conclusion: rules, whatever their source, are needed to contain the "fallen angels" of human nature and make social life livable.

Positive ethics. To transcend these issues and the negativity often linked with ethics, Handelsman, Knapp and Gottlieb (2009) describe positive ethics, which moves the emphasis from following rules and avoiding discipline to aspiring to one's highest ethical ideals, improving ethical decision making. Going beyond "First, do no harm", Corey (2008) distinguishes mandatory from aspirational ethics; aspirational ethics focuses on doing what is in clients' best interests, fitting the client-centred nature of helping, and treats ethics as a way of thinking about becoming the best practitioner possible. Ethical decision making is part of life for helpers and clients, and these values permeate the helping process.
sections.simple: Helping must be ethical and value-driven, so beliefs, values, norms, ethics and morality are an ingredient. Science cannot prove moral values, and people draw them from religion, culture, evolution or pragmatism. Positive or aspirational ethics asks helpers to aim for their highest ideals, not just follow rules.
keyPoints: Helping must be value-driven and ethical to be social-civilising, not just individual-enhancing.
Egan leaves full ethics coverage to dedicated courses and texts (ACA and APA codes; Knapp, 2012; Welfel, 2013).
These concepts are not scientific terms; science cannot prove their validity (Mikulincer and Shaver, 2012).
Sources of morality: religion, culture, bio-social evolution, pragmatism; values are often choices.
Positive ethics (Handelsman, Knapp and Gottlieb, 2009): aspire to highest ideals rather than just avoid discipline.
Corey (2008): mandatory vs aspirational ethics; aspirational ethics serves clients' best interests.

sections.heading: Embracing and Befriending the Uncertainties Inherent in Helping
sections.detailed:
Uncertainty is not itself an ingredient; it pervades all the ingredients. Helpers who understand the uncertainties of the profession are better placed to help clients cope with uncertainty in their own lives.

Why the social sciences are uncertain. The social sciences want to belong to the STEM group and do have elements of all four: they use hard-science research methods where possible, use technologies such as video and the Internet, help clients "reengineer" their lives, and rely on mathematics and statistics. But none of this changes the nature of human behaviour. The probability involved in human behaviour differs radically from that in the hard sciences. Counselling research draws conclusions that are permeated with uncertainties, which researchers list at the end of articles, so findings are hard to translate into practical methods. The relationship Task Force's conclusions, for example, are broad, hard to apply, or sound like common sense. Each ingredient therefore carries its own uncertainties.

The client and the client's context. Karl, like everyone, is complex, and complexity breeds uncertainty. Which past factors are hurting him now? Should he confront problems head on or find ways around them? What outcomes does he want beyond relief from depression and anxiety? Are PTSD symptoms the real issue or do underlying issues matter more? Neither Karl nor Laura can afford to be overwhelmed; with Laura's help Karl must identify the key issues and decide what to do.

The therapist. Laura brings her own culture, personality and approach. She uses the cognitive-behavioural-social-emotional problem-management approach to organise her thinking and also as a "browser" to explore other approaches and draw useful methods and skills, organised within the framework. She is eclectic, but with an organised, client-centred, outcome-oriented eclecticism. Her rich understanding is an asset but brings complexity and thus uncertainty, because methods must be adapted to each client. She must understand Karl before enlisting him to adapt any PTSD programme; PTSD is a package of interrelated symptoms, not a disease, and Karl is Karl, not his symptoms.

The helping relationship. All relationships can be complex and uncertain. The helping relationship must be set up quickly and focused from the start on outcomes, yet it is always a work in progress. Collaboration, done well, reduces uncertainty. Laura has had many such relationships, but everything is new to Karl, and since he is currently out of community, it is unclear how well he can collaborate; helping him into the driver's seat may itself breed more uncertainty.
sections.simple: Uncertainty runs through every ingredient of helping because human behaviour is not predictable like physics. Research findings come with caveats and are hard to apply. Karl's complexity, Laura's rich but eclectic toolkit, and a new, still-forming relationship all add uncertainty.
keyPoints: Uncertainty is not an ingredient but pervades all ingredients.
Social sciences use STEM methods, but human behaviour involves a radically different kind of probability.
Research conclusions carry uncertainties and are hard to translate into practice.
Client complexity (Karl) breeds uncertainty about key issues.
Laura's organised, client-centred, outcome-oriented eclecticism uses problem management as a 'browser'; adapting methods adds uncertainty.
The relationship is always a work in progress; collaboration reduces uncertainty.

sections.heading: Uncertainties in the Therapeutic Dialogue, Two-Way Feedback and the Model of Treatment
sections.detailed:
The therapeutic dialogue. Communication is central to building relationships, yet society does not take communication skills seriously enough to teach them formally or informally. Research shows that many, perhaps most, people believe they communicate better than they actually do. The skills of dialogue (Part II) are complex, and becoming competent is hard. If Karl lacks them, Laura can use her skills to help him engage, but this adds uncertainty. Moreover, uncertainty belongs to the very nature of dialogue: if either party knows the outcome beforehand, it may be a conversation but not a dialogue. In dialogue the parties co-create outcomes. Laura is not treating Karl's PTSD; they are collaborating to make his life more livable.

Two-way feedback. Feedback must be given, explored, confirmed and acted on by both parties, yet its role in therapy has been slow to be recognised and studied. Monitoring session quality and client progress actually reduces uncertainty for both: it is a chance to clear things up. That is why Duncan and his associates use very simple surveys; what matters is not the survey but the consciousness-raising and exploration it promotes. Feedback from helper to client raises its own uncertainty: does it rob clients of autonomy, or amount to a power play or one-upmanship that helpers try to avoid?

The model or method of treatment and its assumptions. There are hundreds of approaches, all claiming effectiveness. Laura uses the problem-management framework to suggest methods drawn from many approaches, but not in a "let's try this and see" way. Knowing many evidence-based approaches does not clutter her mind because the framework organises them. She makes sure Karl understands what is on offer without dumping this complexity on him.
sections.simple: Dialogue is uncertain by nature because both people co-create the outcome, and most people overrate their own communication skills. Feedback reduces uncertainty by clearing things up, though helper feedback raises questions about autonomy. Laura handles the many treatment options by organising them through the problem-management framework, without overloading Karl.
keyPoints: Society neglects communication skills, and most people overrate their own communication ability.
True dialogue co-creates outcomes; if the outcome is known in advance it is not dialogue.
Feedback reduces uncertainty; simple surveys matter for the exploration they prompt.
Helper-to-client feedback raises uncertainty about autonomy and power plays.
Laura organises many evidence-based approaches with the problem-management framework and spares Karl the complexity.

sections.heading: Uncertainties in Problem Management, Decision Making and the Beliefs-Values-Norms-Ethics-Morality Factors
sections.detailed:
The standard problem-management process as a human universal. Although most approaches use problem-management language, the profession has not openly recognised its importance; research on problem management is more likely in business schools than psychology departments. Karl's familiarity with the process reduces complexity. The process is a map, but the map is not the territory: Karl and his life are the territory. Laura knows both from experience, but they must chart a course together, agree on changes, accept twists, stops and starts, and sometimes even change the destination. Hence collaboration and feedback matter. The many evidence-based approaches to anxiety, depression and PTSD could add uncertainty, but Laura uses the framework as browser, sorter and organiser.

Decision making as a human universal. On the surface decision making is a rational choice among researched options (Galotti, 2002), but it has many pitfalls (Ariely; Chabris and Simons; Kahneman; March; Van Hecke; Watts). In Thinking, Fast and Slow, Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman (2012) describes System One, fast, intuitive and emotional, with its capabilities, faults and biases; people are swayed by intuitive impressions and boast of following their gut, often to disaster, so it matters to know when intuition can be trusted. System Two is slow, deliberative and logical and can produce life-enhancing decisions. Karl's gut decision to leave the army proved life-enhancing, but his quick dismissal of the feedback surveys did not serve him. Decision making mixes rational and irrational elements like fudge-ripple ice cream. Helpers help clients climb out of decisional pits or avoid them. Karl admits cutting himself off from family and friends was a mistake; getting back into community is a decision that requires many more decisions, and he will not move linearly through the rational model. Karl tends to decide quickly with little reflection, so Laura thinks it useful to help him review what kind of decision maker he is.

The beliefs-values-norms-ethics-morality factors. Rogerson and associates (2011), in American Psychologist, argue that current ethical decision-making models are overly rational and ignore nonrational factors such as context, perceptions, relationships and emotions, and that ethics should be reconceptualised. Karl is a semi-lapsed fundamentalist; aspects of that belief system still cling to him, and he says he sometimes prays when angry. Laura sees this as positive, recalling research on prayer's value in controlling anger and aggression (Bremner, Koole and Bushman, 2011); for her the issue is what works, not the belief system. Decisions are driven by beliefs and values, so they must attend to what underpins Karl's decisions, such as guilt and being "out of community". Helping is about managing problems and developing opportunities, not personality transformation; Karl will always be Karl. He is the expert on himself despite blind spots, and he, not abnormal psychology textbooks, is the best source of knowledge about himself. Laura helps him through uncertainties without being paralysed by them.

The upside of uncertainty. Duncan (2010) describes uncertainty as the place of unlimited possibilities for change, giving therapy its texture and excitement of discovery, allowing aha moments and new insights. Orlinsky and Rønnestad (2005) show that the helper's tolerance for complexity and uncertainty is vital. Egan prefers that therapists, and eventually clients, befriend and embrace uncertainty and learn from it, since human behaviour will always be uncertain.
sections.simple: The problem-management process is a map, but each client's life is a different territory, so the route must be worked out together. Decisions mix fast gut thinking (System One) and slow logical thinking (System Two), and are driven by beliefs and values. Uncertainty is not just a threat: Duncan sees it as the source of new possibilities, and helpers should embrace it.
keyPoints: Problem management is a map, not the territory; the client's life is the territory.
Kahneman (2012): System One is fast, intuitive, emotional and bias-prone; System Two is slow and deliberate.
Decision making mixes rational and irrational elements; clients rarely move linearly.
Rogerson et al. (2011): ethical decision models ignore nonrational factors such as context, relationships and emotion.
Prayer can help control anger and aggression (Bremner, Koole and Bushman, 2011).
Uncertainty is a source of possibility (Duncan, 2010); tolerance for it is vital (Orlinsky and Rønnestad, 2005).

sections.heading: Moving from Smart to Wise: Managing the Shadow Side of Helping
sections.detailed:
Egan adds one more dimension of uncertainty. Intelligence alone is not enough to build a constructive relationship and use the framework well; "smart is not smart enough". The helper must also be wise. Wise helpers understand the limitations of theories, frameworks and models, and of helpers, the profession, clients and the environments affecting helping. It is one thing to handle the "known unknowns" covered under uncertainty; it is another to deal with the "unknown unknowns" lurking behind all human endeavours. These make up the shadow side of life.

Definition. The shadow side of helping consists of all the things that substantially affect the helping relationship, process and outcomes, usually adversely but sometimes constructively, yet are not identified and explored by the helper, the client or even the profession.

Examples. All human endeavours have a shadow side. Companies suffer internal politics and covert or vaguely understood beliefs, values and norms that do not serve the business, customers, employees or shareholders; in the worldwide financial crisis, shady dealings went on for years before collapse. In the helping professions, models are flawed; helpers are sometimes selfish, lazy, even predatory, and prone to burnout; clients too can be selfish, lazy and predatory, even within the relationship.

Benefits if managed wisely. Egan likens the shadow side to "noise" in a system. Scientists find a small amount of noise, called stochastic resonance, can make a system more sensitive and efficient. Debate about what makes helping effective can likewise benefit clients, but sometimes the noise gets too loud.

Infighting. There are conflicts in the profession close to internecine wars. The debate over the "correct" approach to diversity and multiculturalism brings out the best and worst, with accusations of cultural imperialism on one side and political correctness on the other. Debates on whether the professions should take political stands or engage in social engineering produce more heat than light, and every significant article draws testy replies. The search for truth sometimes yields to the need to be right, and clients are often left out. Just as businesses reinvent themselves starting from customers, the helping professions should keep reinventing themselves by looking through clients' eyes.

Irrationality. If the world were rational there would be no clients; many people knowingly head into trouble. Life is more maze than straight road, mixing good and evil, comedy and tragedy, cowardice and heroism. The book describes helping in very positive terms, as it could or should be, not always as it is.

Wise helpers. They are idealistic without being naive and choose realism over cynicism. Not knowing what is in the shadows is naive; believing shadow-side realities usually win is cynical. Egan describes a cynic as someone who has given up but not yet shut up. Wise helpers pursue upbeat, compassionate realism and see the journey from smart to wise as never-ending, while still cultivating the "smart" part: separating sense from nonsense, as in John Ruscio's (2005) Critical Thinking in Psychology.

The book is not a treatise on the shadow side but aims to get helpers thinking about it. Signs that the professions are starting to explore it include What Therapists Don't Talk About and Why (Pope, Sonne and Greene, 2006), which examines myths and taboos blocking effective helping. Egan believes the professions must become more self-critical in a positive way, and doubts science will ever eliminate the shadow side of life.
sections.simple: Being smart is not enough; good helpers must be wise. The shadow side is everything that affects helping but goes unnoticed and undiscussed: flawed models, selfish or burnt-out helpers, manipulative clients and professional infighting. Wise helpers are idealistic but not naive, realistic but not cynical, practising upbeat, compassionate realism.
keyPoints: 'Smart is not smart enough': helpers must move from smart to wise.
Shadow side: unidentified, unexplored factors that substantially (usually adversely) affect helping relationships, processes and outcomes.
Known unknowns (uncertainties) vs unknown unknowns (the shadow side).
Shadow side includes flawed models, selfish, lazy, predatory or burnt-out helpers, similar clients, and professional infighting.
Stochastic resonance: a little noise can improve a system, but too much harms.
Wise helpers are idealistic but not naive, realistic but not cynical; they practise upbeat, compassionate realism and critical thinking (Ruscio, 2005; Pope, Sonne and Greene, 2006).

terms.definition: Professionals whose official role is to help people manage life's distressing problems, such as counsellors, psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers and ministers of religion.
Non-professionals such as friends, relatives, bartenders, hairdressers and even strangers who help people with problems in living; most help-seekers turn to them.
Egan's preferred term for the person seeking or needing help, chosen over 'patient' to sidestep the medical-model dispute.
Complex, messy, emotionally charged problems in living that clients are not handling well and that usually lack clear-cut solutions.
Resources and possibilities clients are not using; a second starting point for helping focused on what could be better rather than what is wrong.
Seligman and Csikszentmihalyi's call to study strength and virtue and nurture what is best, not just treat pathology; Ince called it the science of satisfaction.
Approach promoted by Duncan, Miller and associates that puts clients in charge and uses outcomes to guide helping.
Helping clients manage problems more effectively and develop unused resources and opportunities in ways that improve their lives.

terms.term: Goal Two: learning how to help oneself
terms.definition: Helping clients become better at helping themselves in everyday life by passing on problem-management skills.
Helping clients develop an action-oriented habit of anticipating problem situations rather than only managing them after they arise.
Sherwood and Glidewell's conflict-management model: small unspoken annoyances (pinches) saved up eventually explode into major blowups (crunches).
Term used by many writers for the essential elements found across all successful therapies.
Egan's term for the interactive elements that produce life-enhancing outcomes; preferred over 'factors' because his list goes beyond the usual research lists.
Egan's description of the helper's role: facilitating change for which the client is responsible.
Egan's metaphor for clients being in charge of managing their own problems; helpers help them get there and stay there.
Helper-client conversation in which communication skills are marshalled so that both parties co-create outcomes.
Continuous monitoring, by both client and helper, of client progress toward outcomes and of how well sessions contribute to them.
Egan's view that helping is inescapably a two-way influence process that neither removes the client from the driver's seat nor makes the helper a victim of client whims.
The quality of a treatment model that makes sense and looks as if it might work.
Research term for legitimate treatment approaches (e.g., for PTSD), each with merit, though one may suit a particular client better.
Egan's generic helping process built on four questions: What's going on? What does a better future look like? How do I get there? How do I make it happen?
The client's account of the problems, concerns and undeveloped opportunities to be worked on.
The client's picture of a better future, including the changes and goals that would manage the problem situation.
The plan and actions needed to turn the preferred picture into reality.
The broad and specific actions clients take to produce change; the ongoing challenge of making it all happen.
A process found across cultures and embedded in human beings (McCrae and Costa; Norenzayan and Heine); Egan applies it to problem management and decision making.
Orlinsky and Howard's term for a framework common to helping in general; Egan applies it to problem management.
Step-wise decision model: problem identification and information gathering, analysis, making a choice, follow through.
Describing accurately the issue being decided, as part of problem identification and information gathering.
The interactive shared beliefs, values and norms of a group's members.
Approach reviewed by Handelsman, Knapp and Gottlieb that shifts from following rules and avoiding discipline to aspiring to one's highest ethical ideals.
Corey's distinction between minimum required ethical conduct and ethics aimed at doing what is in clients' best interests and becoming the best practitioner possible.
Not an ingredient itself but a quality pervading all ingredients of helping, arising from the nature of human behaviour.
Laura's use of the problem-management framework as a browser to draw methods from many approaches in an organised, client-centred, outcome-oriented way.
Kahneman's two decision systems: fast, intuitive and emotional thinking versus slow, deliberative and logical thinking.
Recognised uncertainties of helping versus hidden factors lurking behind all human endeavours, which make up the shadow side.

All those things that substantially affect the helping relationship, process and outcomes, usually adversely but sometimes constructively, yet go unidentified and unexplored by helper, client or profession.
Scientific finding that a small amount of noise can make a system more sensitive and efficient; Egan's analogy for wisely managed shadow-side debate.
The stance of wise helpers: idealistic without being naive, realistic without being cynical.

people.name: Swindle, Heller, Pescosolido and Kikuzawa (2000)
